lines.text: Take two phones, identical in every way.
lines.event: two phones drawn white on the balance pans

lines.text: Charge one completely, drain the other until it's dead,
lines.visual_cue: battery glyphs on screens: full / empty
lines.event: coral block fills the left phone's battery

lines.text: and set them on a balance.
lines.event: balance drawn around the phones

lines.text: The charged phone is heavier.
lines.event: punch-in: exaggerated tilt wedge on the left pan

lines.text: Not by any amount you could measure.
lines.visual_cue: tiny question mark by the tilt
lines.event: note: 'heavier by ???'

lines.text: Yet nothing material went in while it charged.
lines.event: charging cable drawn to the left phone

lines.text: No atoms came down the cable.
lines.event: note: '0 atoms in'

lines.text: No extra electrons piled up either: every electron that flowed in through one wire flowed back out through the other.
lines.event: electron loop arrows along the cable

lines.text: The only thing the phone gained was energy.
lines.visual_cue: energy block glows into the battery
lines.event: colour flood: coral ENERGY block enters the phone

lines.text: And energy, it turns out, has weight.
lines.visual_cue: the coral block sits on the pan
lines.event: the energy block becomes the mystery; chapter capsule

lines.text: Inside the battery, charging doesn't add stuff. It rearranges it.
lines.event: battery cross-section drawn (holes as layers)

lines.text: Ions shuttle between two layers into an arrangement that stores energy, like a stretched spring.
lines.event: ions + arrows between the two electrode layers

lines.text: Use the phone, and they slide back down, releasing it.
lines.event: discharge arrows (grey) opposite the coral charge arrows

lines.text: A full battery and an empty one hold exactly the same atoms.
lines.event: note: 'same atoms, same electrons'

lines.text: The only difference is energy.
lines.event: swatch strip states tracked

lines.text: So why would energy have weight at all?
lines.event: camera drifts up; the question written large

lines.text: Matter is supposed to be the thing that weighs.
lines.event: half-coloured block left; transition drift right

lines.text: For a century, science's most careful weighings said the opposite:
lines.event: new region: 1770s Paris lab table

lines.text: nothing inside a sealed container can change its weight.
lines.event: sealed glass vessel with tin block inside

lines.text: The rule was born in Paris, in the seventeen seventies, with Antoine Lavoisier, a chemist who trusted his balance more than any theory.
lines.sub: The rule was born in Paris, in the 1770s, with Antoine Lavoisier, a chemist who trusted his balance more than any theory.
lines.event: handwritten label + leader line

lines.text: He sealed tin inside a glass vessel, melting the glass shut so nothing could get in or out, and took its weight.
lines.event: vessel neck sealed; note written

lines.text: Then he heated it, until part of the shiny metal turned to grey powder, let it cool, and took its weight again.
lines.event: flame + mustard heat waves through the glass

lines.text: Heat had poured in and out. The weight had not changed at all.
lines.event: both balance readings match; coral 'unchanged!'

lines.text: In seventeen eighty-nine, his rule: an equal quantity of matter, before and after.
lines.sub: In 1789, his rule: an equal quantity of matter, before and after.
lines.event: note card: the conservation rule, coral underline

lines.text: Energy, it seemed, weighs nothing.
lines.event: swatch strip: 'energy weighs nothing?'

lines.text: But a rule is only as good as the balance that tests it.
lines.event: new region: Berlin, 1890s

lines.text: In the eighteen nineties, Hans Landolt in Berlin spent twenty years testing it harder than anyone.
lines.sub: In the 1890s, Hans Landolt in Berlin spent 20 years testing it harder than anyone.
lines.event: label + two-decade calendar note

lines.text: Two chemicals, sealed in the separate arms of a glass vessel, react;
lines.event: H-vessel drawn; coral + mustard chemicals in the arms

lines.text: the heat escapes; he weighs it again. And again. And again.
lines.event: colour flood: chemicals merge mottled; heat arrows rise; weigh ticks

lines.text: He chased every error — buoyancy, moisture, dust.
lines.event: error-hunting list written

lines.text: His nineteen oh eight verdict: no reaction changed weight by more than three hundredths of a milligram.
lines.sub: His 1908 verdict: no reaction changed weight by more than 0.03 mg.
lines.event: punch-in on the needle; coral circle around '0.03 mg'

lines.text: If the escaping heat weighed anything at all, it weighed less than that.
lines.event: error bar drawn under the needle

lines.text: Then a tiny glowing sample made that answer hard to believe.
lines.event: new region: back in Paris, 1902

lines.text: Radium, which Marie Curie purified in nineteen oh two, from more than a ton of ore.
lines.sub: Radium, which Marie Curie purified in 1902, from more than a ton of ore.
lines.event: purification chain drawn: ton of ore into one vial

lines.text: Pierre Curie measured one gram giving off a hundred calories of heat, every hour.
lines.event: heat waves radiate; '100 cal/hour' note

lines.text: That adds up to nearly nine hundred thousand calories a year.
lines.event: calendar pages drawn flying; radium bar grows tall (coral)

lines.text: A gram of coal gives seven thousand. Then it's gone.
lines.sub: A gram of coal gives 7,000. Then it's gone.
lines.event: coal bar stays tiny (graphite); swatch strip records both

lines.text: The radium releases a hundred times more, every year, and barely slows down:
lines.event: coral '×100' bursts between the bars

lines.text: half is still there sixteen hundred years from now.
lines.event: decay line drawn; 'half remains at 1,600 years'

lines.text: Nobody could say what it was using up.
lines.event: big '?' over the glowing vial

lines.text: Either it soaked up invisible energy from space, or the energy came from inside the atom itself.
lines.event: option A: sky-to-vial arrow; option B: atom cross-section

lines.text: The first clue had appeared earlier, in the way light behaves.
lines.event: new region: light, 1900

lines.text: In nineteen hundred, Henri Poincaré worked through a fact most people never think about: light pushes.
lines.sub: In 1900, Henri Poincaré worked through a fact most people never think about: light pushes.
lines.event: sun + radiating light rays drawn

lines.text: It's why a comet's tail points away from the Sun;
lines.event: comet + tail pushed outward

lines.text: and lab experiments had just measured that push.
lines.event: light-pressure apparatus: beam pushing a vane

lines.text: Anything that pushes carries momentum.
lines.event: note: 'push = momentum'

lines.text: A flash of energy E carries momentum: E divided by the speed of light.
lines.event: handwritten: 'momentum = E / c'

lines.text: Momentum is mass times speed.
lines.event: handwritten: 'momentum = mass × speed'

lines.text: What mass would that flash need? Its energy, divided by the speed of light squared.
lines.event: match cut + punch-in: 'mass = E / c²' in coral

lines.text: His example: a one kilogram lamp firing three million joules of light recoils like a cannon,
lines.event: lamp fires a flash; recoil arrow '1 cm/s'

lines.text: while the flash carries thirty-three billionths of a gram.
lines.event: flash labelled '33 billionths of a gram'

lines.text: But he called it a fiction, not a real weight.
lines.event: 'a fictitious fluid' — quote note beside the number

lines.text: The number sat there. He didn't believe it.
lines.event: the coral formula left half-coloured; transition drift

lines.text: Believing it took Albert Einstein — twenty six, a clerk at the patent office in Bern.
lines.sub: Believing it took Albert Einstein — 26, a clerk at the patent office in Bern.
lines.event: new region: Bern, 1905; desk + patent doodles

lines.text: In nineteen oh five, just after finishing relativity, he wrote to a friend:
lines.sub: In 1905, just after finishing relativity, he wrote to a friend:
lines.event: letter card drawn with the claim

lines.text: a body's mass must be a measure of the energy inside it.
lines.event: coral underline under the claim

lines.text: Light carries mass, he said. Radium should get noticeably lighter.
lines.event: small radium vial with down-arrow

lines.text: That September, three pages in the leading physics journal.
lines.event: paper with '3 pages' note

lines.text: A glowing object, at rest, fires two identical flashes in opposite directions.
lines.event: glowing dot; two mustard flashes left/right

lines.text: The pushes cancel. It just loses the light's energy, L.
lines.event: 'L' labels both flashes; arrows cancel

lines.text: Now watch from a passing train.
lines.event: match cut: same drawing, train + motion lines

lines.text: The speed is unchanged, but the forward flash now looks slightly more energetic, the backward slightly less.
lines.event: forward flash redrawn longer, backward shorter

lines.text: Add them: most of the difference cancels. Not all.
lines.event: energy bookkeeping: 'L + a little extra'

lines.text: From the train, the light carries away a little more than L.
lines.event: coral highlight on the extra

lines.text: That extra must come out of its kinetic energy.
lines.event: note: 'paid out of kinetic energy'

lines.text: And kinetic energy is one half, times mass, times speed squared.
lines.event: handwritten: 'kinetic = ½ · mass · speed²'

lines.text: The speed hasn't changed. So the mass drops —
lines.event: 'speed' crossed out; 'mass?' remains

lines.text: by the light's energy, divided by the speed of light squared.
lines.event: punch-in: the same coral formula, re-registered solid

lines.text: A year later, Einstein offered a simpler argument: a flash of light inside a box.
lines.event: new region: a box floats in space; starfield dots

lines.text: Walk from one end of a small boat to the other, and it slides back under you.
lines.event: boat + walking figure; slide arrows

lines.text: Nothing inside a closed system can move its own centre of mass.
lines.event: centre-of-mass dot + fixed axis drawn

lines.text: Now make it a box in empty space, and make you a flash of light off the left wall.
lines.event: colour flood: the boat block becomes the box

lines.text: The flash pushes the box back, crosses, and is absorbed at the right wall —
lines.event: box recoil arrow; flash travels (dashed); absorption burst

lines.text: the box stops, shifted. Nothing outside touched it.
lines.event: ruler shows the shift d; note 'nothing outside'

lines.text: So either the box pushed itself through space, or the light carried mass, wall to wall.
lines.event: option notes: 'magic push' vs 'light carries mass'

lines.text: The boat settles it: box mass times shift equals light mass times box length.
lines.event: handwritten: 'M·d = m·L'

lines.text: Everything cancels but one line: the light's mass equals its energy, divided by the speed of light squared.
lines.event: punch-in: 'm = E / c²' in a coral box

lines.text: The left wall really gets lighter. The right wall really gets heavier.
lines.event: left wall block fades lighter, right wall heavier

lines.text: Einstein credited Poincaré on the paper's first page.
lines.event: note: 'built on Poincaré's reasoning'

lines.text: Once energy has real weight, the old mysteries make sense.
lines.event: new region: the fraction

lines.text: Only one thing hid that weight: the size of c squared.
lines.event: 'c' written, squared

lines.text: Light moves at three hundred million metres per second.
lines.event: handwritten: 'c = 300,000,000 m/s'

lines.text: So c squared is ninety million billion.
Ninety million billion joules, for one kilogram of weight.
lines.event: the fraction: tiny E over a huge graphite slab

lines.text: Landolt's escaping heat weighed about a billionth of a gram.
lines.event: swatch strip: reaction heat, a billionth g

lines.text: His balance could only see thirty millionths of a gram.
lines.sub: His balance could only see 30 millionths of a gram.
lines.event: swatch strip: balance sees 30 millionths g

lines.text: Tens of thousands of times too coarse.
lines.event: coral '×30,000 too coarse' between swatches

lines.text: Even a gram of radium radiates a whole year of heat that weighs just forty billionths of a gram,
lines.event: capsule drawn; 12-month dial around it

lines.text: right at the edge of the finest balances — after twelve patient months.
lines.event: needle drawn a hair off zero; 'a full year' note

lines.text: So could anyone weigh energy at all?
lines.event: new region: Cambridge, 1932

lines.text: It would take more energy per atom, and a way to weigh single atoms.
lines.event: two notes: 'more energy per atom' / 'weigh single atoms'

lines.text: Both arrived in Rutherford's lab in Cambridge.
lines.event: vacuum chamber + magnet poles drawn

lines.text: Atoms were no longer weighed on pans: flying through magnetic fields in a vacuum, the lighter ones curve more sharply. The bend became the scale.
lines.event: dashed arcs: light atom bends hard, heavy bends less

lines.text: On the fourteenth of April, nineteen thirty-two, researchers fired fast protons at a thin layer of lithium.
lines.sub: On the 14th of April 1932, researchers fired fast protons at a thin layer of lithium.
lines.event: proton beam from left; thin lithium target

lines.text: One watched from a darkened hut beneath the machine, shielded from X-rays.
lines.event: hut drawn under the machine; observer figure inside

lines.text: The screen lit up.
lines.event: particle sparkles burst on the screen

lines.text: Rutherford squeezed in: the flashes looked, he said, mighty like alpha particles.
lines.event: quote card: 'mighty like alpha particles'

lines.text: A lithium nucleus had swallowed a proton and split into two helium nuclei,
lines.event: match cut: magnified reaction; lithium swallows proton

lines.text: flying apart with seventeen point two million electron volts.
lines.sub: flying apart with 17.2 million electron volts.
lines.event: shatter: two alpha particles burst apart with energy arrows

lines.text: Lithium plus hydrogen outweighs two heliums.
lines.event: ledger: 'Li + H > He + He'

lines.text: If Einstein was right, the missing mass times c squared must equal that energy.
lines.event: coral '=' drawn between missing mass and energy

lines.text: But lithium's nineteen thirty-two mass predicted only fourteen million electron volts, against seventeen.
lines.sub: But lithium's 1932 mass predicted only 14 million electron volts, against 17.
lines.event: bar: predicted 14 vs measured 17.2; 'blurry'

lines.text: A year later, a more precise lithium mass raised the prediction to sixteen point eight — within a few percent. It matched.
lines.sub: A year later, a more precise lithium mass raised the prediction to 16.8 — within a few percent. It matched.
lines.event: bar re-registered: 16.8 close to 17.2; check mark

lines.text: Weighing atoms had already explained something bigger.
lines.event: new region: the stars

lines.text: In nineteen twenty, helium proved lighter than the four hydrogens that build it.
lines.sub: In 1920, helium proved lighter than the four hydrogens that build it.
lines.event: four pale hydrogen circles drawn

lines.text: Four point zero three one three, against four point zero zero two six.
lines.event: handwritten ledger: '4.0313 to 4.0026'

lines.text: Arthur Eddington saw that the missing mass could power the stars.
lines.event: small telescope doodle; label 'Eddington, 1920'

lines.text: Fusing hydrogen into helium leaves seven tenths of one percent missing, carried away as energy.
lines.event: four H merge into one He; a coral chip flies off

lines.text: The Sun fuses six hundred million tons of hydrogen a second,
lines.sub: The Sun fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen a second,
lines.event: sun with rays; '600,000,000 t/s' note

lines.text: and four million tons of that never becomes matter — it leaves as light.
lines.sub: and 4 million tons of that never becomes matter — it leaves as light.
lines.event: rays leave; '4,000,000 t/s' in coral

lines.text: The same equation runs the stars, and the battery in your pocket.
lines.event: tiny phone doodle beside the sun; coral link

lines.text: So, back to the phones.
lines.event: match cut: the ch1 balance region, aged

lines.text: The charged one gained energy, and therefore mass: less than a billionth of a gram.
lines.visual_cue: phone on the pan, tiny block
lines.event: charged phone redrawn; coral energy block on the pan

lines.text: No balance can show it. We know it anyway:
lines.event: the tilt wedge again; 'unmeasurable' note

lines.text: every kind of energy weighs exactly its amount, divided by c squared.
lines.event: the equation written large, mustard block under 'mc²'

lines.text: Almost all the mass of your body is energy too, locked in its protons and neutrons.
lines.event: body outline drawn; match cut: magnifier with a proton

lines.text: The three quarks in a proton are less than one percent of its weight.
lines.event: three small dots in the proton; '<1%' note

lines.text: The rest is the strong force — trapped, seething motion.
lines.event: colour flood: the proton floods with energy texture

lines.text: You are mostly stored energy, wearing the shape of a person. So is your phone.
lines.event: the body and phone blocks re-registered to coral

lines.text: Charge it tonight, and in the morning, it will be ever so slightly heavier.
lines.event: camera settles: phone, balance, E = mc²; end card drawn
